cells.tense: You're the one keeping the form, and choosing the pace is part of the work.
cells.ask: Put one piece of the design on the table in front of someone today — say it plainly, without the whole plan built out — and watch whether hearing it come back in their words makes it more real to you.
cells.core:
The design holds because you keep it holding — some days that's one sketch, one sentence said at the right time, watching the structure carry weight no one else knew was on it. Care for growth and form sit together in how you work, not as a fight but as a turn of habit you've made. What you carry is both what you're protecting and what you're building next.

When you go to put one piece out, it can feel like too much because it isn't all of it yet. It doesn't have to be all of it. Handing one part over today is how you find out it was real, and what comes back tells you more than the whole plan in your head ever did.

cells.tense: You're already out past the work — seeing how the shape will hold before anyone can see it with you.
cells.ask: Write the future version on one page today and leave it there — a single page, not the whole system — and see what the day feels like once it's down and you've walked away from it.
cells.core:
Ahead of the work, you're guarding the shape — checking whether it's clear enough, whether the people around are reading it right, whether it'll hold when it has to. The reach isn't the ambition. It's how much goes into protecting the form so it can't be mistaken, and that's the part that costs you the thing form was for.

The page is enough. Put it where you can see it and stop for the day — not because the plan is done, but because a design that can't be slept on is one you're carrying awake. Letting it sit for a night gives the shape back some room, and tomorrow the next step is easier to see without bracing.

cells.tense: The door where you last put shape to this is behind you, and you haven't gone back through it.
cells.ask: Make the shape visible to one other person today — tape a diagram where one person will see it, or say one step aloud to someone — and notice afterward whether it felt more like reaching or more like guarding.
cells.core:
Putting shape to a thing has gone quiet, though care for what you're making hasn't stopped. You still know how a thing holds — what it takes, where it wobbles, what to leave alone. What's missing is a piece of it meeting someone else's eyes, and that's the move the work runs on when it's going well: one sketch shown, one step said aloud, one person seeing the shape and asking a question about it.

The showing has gone quiet, and anything you've made lately may have stopped getting seen. Making the shape visible is what brings the rest of it back, and it doesn't have to be neat or complete. What comes back — a question, a shrug, a nod — tells you where the shape actually stands.

One move, toward one person, today. Small enough to do at the table you're sitting at. Whatever lands, landing is the point; it's easier to tend the next thing once you know which side of the shape you're standing on.

cells.tense: You're keeping something steady right now and treating the keeping as nothing worth saying.
cells.ask: Name one thing you built the shape of — and say out loud to one person today, in plain words, that you're the one who kept it holding.
cells.core:
The shape holds because you keep checking it — where it wobbles, what to leave alone, what the next step is. That's the part of this that works: care for the thing shows up in the watching, and it's been showing up for a while without anyone saying so. When it's going well, the check is quiet and the work is plain — a glance at the structure, a small correction, an eye that keeps things from drifting.

By your own account none of it's yours — it happened through the work, it was obvious, anyone would have done it. But watch what you notice, which problems you see coming, how you keep things from wobbling. That's tending doing its work without a name.

One true sentence to one person, today. Not a claim over anything. Just what you actually did. When the effort is said out loud once, it can end somewhere instead of running on in the dark, and something loosens that hasn't been able to.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending something steadily and calling it nothing.

attempts.check: The draft names a moment where a person keeps going without saying so, and a cost it carries — but it never says why the silence was learned or when, and I've kept it out; the person may catch what matters to them, or not, and the ask stands either way. The four "check" particulars: 1) The unsupported claim is that the person built the thing and is quiet about that — the record's Unacknowledged general fact is operating without awareness, and the specificity of a doing-something-and-not-saying-it is my read, not their report; stated as something to put down, not as fact about their history. 2) A reader might say what looks like understating is really just holding it lightly, not steering under cover, and the ask — say one piece out loud — survives that because it still tests something true either way. 3) The ask survives my being wrong because the action itself is a fact about the day, not proof of a wound. 4) The line that serves the writer over the reader is 'the record calls that confidence' — a self-confirming sentence that flatters Celeste Sun and gives the person nothing to use.
